title: ML & AI Fundamentals for Engineers
summary: Machine learning is writing programs that learn the rules from data instead of you hard-coding them — and most of the job is data, evaluation, and serving, not math.

blocks.markdown:
ML is showing a program lots of examples so it figures out the rule, instead of you hand-coding it.

- The learned rule is a **model** — a function with adjustable knobs.
- **Training** nudges those knobs until guesses are mostly right; then it **predicts** on new inputs.
- The whole point is **generalization** — working on data it never saw, not memorizing.
- Most of the real effort is **data, evaluation, and serving**, not the math.

blocks.subTitle: Which model to reach for
blocks.markdown:
Pick the simplest model that clears the bar.

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Predict a number | Linear regression |
| Predict yes/no or a class | Logistic regression, then trees |
| Tabular, accuracy fast | Gradient-boosted trees |
| Images, audio, text | Neural networks |
| No labels, find groups | Clustering |

blocks.subTitle: The pipeline
blocks.markdown:
ML is a loop, not a one-shot build.

- **Collect data** — labeled examples; garbage data caps your ceiling.
- **Build features** — turn raw data into measurable numeric properties.
- **Train** — nudge parameters to lower the loss.
- **Evaluate** — check on data the model never trained on.
- **Deploy** — serve predictions behind an API.
- **Monitor & retrain** — accuracy decays as the world shifts, so you refresh.

blocks.subTitle: Three learning paradigms
blocks.markdown:
How a model learns depends on what signal it gets.

- **Supervised** — labeled input to answer pairs; splits into **regression** (numbers) and **classification** (categories). ~90% of industry ML.
- **Unsupervised** — no labels; finds structure via **clustering** or **dimensionality reduction**.
- **Reinforcement** — an **agent** takes actions, gets **rewards**, learns a policy by trial and error. Powerful but data-hungry; rare in backend work.

blocks.subTitle: Training: guess, measure, nudge
blocks.markdown:
Training is repeated "guess, measure error, nudge knobs downhill."

- The model starts with random parameters and terrible guesses.
- A **loss function** measures how wrong it is.
- **Gradient descent** computes which way to nudge each parameter and takes a small step.
- The **learning rate** sets step size — too big overshoots, too small crawls.
- One full pass over the data is an **epoch**; repeat many times until loss flattens.

blocks.subTitle: Train / validation / test split
blocks.markdown:
You can't grade a model on data it studied — everyone scores 100% and you learn nothing.

- **Training set** (~60%) — the model learns its parameters here.
- **Validation set** (~20%) — tune **hyperparameters** and pick between models.
- **Test set** (~20%) — touched **once**, at the very end, for an honest number.
- **k-fold cross-validation** rotates the validation slice across k chunks and averages — better when data is scarce.

blocks.subTitle: Overfitting & bias-variance
blocks.markdown:
Two ways a model fails, and the dial between them.

- **Underfitting** — too simple to capture the pattern; bad on both train and test (**high bias**).
- **Overfitting** — memorizes training noise; great on train, bad on new data (**high variance**).
- **Bias-variance trade-off** — total error ≈ bias² + variance + noise; lowering one often raises the other.
- Fight overfitting with **more data**, **simpler models**, **regularization**, and **early stopping**.

blocks.subTitle: Why accuracy lies
blocks.markdown:
With imbalanced classes, accuracy is a trap: if 99% of cases are legit, "always legit" is 99% accurate and catches zero fraud.

- **Precision** = TP / (TP + FP) — of what you flagged, how many were real? Few false alarms.
- **Recall** = TP / (TP + FN) — of all real positives, how many caught? Few misses.
- **F1** = harmonic mean of precision and recall — one balanced number.
- **AUC** — ranking quality across all thresholds, independent of class balance.

blocks.subTitle: What you trade on
blocks.markdown:
Model choice is mostly picking which axis to give up.

| Trade | Driven by |
|---|---|
| Accuracy vs interpretability | Must you explain decisions? |
| Simple vs complex | How much clean data? |
| Precision vs recall | Cost of a false alarm vs a miss |
| ML vs rules | Does a heuristic already work? |

blocks.subTitle: Decision rules
blocks.markdown:
Plain-English defaults before you reach for ML.

- **If a simple rule works, use it** — don't ML for ML's sake.
- **Tabular + want accuracy fast** → gradient-boosted trees.
- **Images, audio, text, lots of data** → neural networks.
- **Must explain every decision** → logistic regression or a shallow tree.
- **Always build a dumb baseline first** (predict the majority class). If your fancy model can't beat it, something's wrong.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
The model choice usually follows a constraint, not raw accuracy.

- **Gmail spam** — tuned for **high precision** (real mail in spam is costly) and constantly retrained as spammers adapt.
- **Credit scoring** — uses **logistic regression** because regulators demand explainability, even if deep nets score higher.
- **Uber ETA** — gradient-boosted trees plus a **feature store** that serves identical features to training and live inference.
- **Netflix** — the win came from blending models and optimizing the whole system, not one clever model.

blocks.subTitle: Production signals
blocks.markdown:
ML systems are operational — these are the signals you watch.

- **Live metrics vs offline.** A big drop means **training/serving skew** or drift.
- **Input feature drift.** Leading indicator of accuracy decay, visible before labels arrive.
- **Tail latency.** An accurate model at 500ms is useless in a 50ms path.
- **Business metric, not just model score.** Score up while revenue flatlines is a red flag.
- **Model + data lineage.** Know which version produced each prediction so you can roll back fast.

The mistakes that bite in interviews and production:

- **"High accuracy means it's good."** Under imbalance, check the rare important class.
- **"The test set is just more validation data."** One decision based on it contaminates it — lock it away, touch it once.
- **"Training accuracy is what matters."** It can be made perfect by overfitting; the train-vs-validation gap is the alarm.
- **"The model is the project."** Data, features, and serving cause most failures.
- **"Correlation = causation."** Models exploit correlations, not causes — act on that and you can be badly misled.
